newsitem.title: TANZANIA: IMF team optimistic over Tanzania reforms.
newsitem.headline: IMF team optimistic over Tanzania reforms.

text.p: The International Monetary Fund (IMF) said on Wednesday it was optimistic an IMF mission to Tanzania would be satisfied with economic reforms which are needed for a new series of soft loans.
The IMF team arrived on Sunday to assess privatisation and restructuring of the state-owned National Bank of Commerce (NBC), IMF Tanzania representative Festus Osunsade told Reuters.

"The key issue is a review of government budgetary operations and on the structural side privatisation, civil service retrenchment and the restructuring of the NBC. Both sides are optimistic the review will go well," Osunsade said.
"The purpose of the mission is to review Tanzania's performance under ESAF as a precondition for the next disbursement," he added.
Last November the IMF approved an Enhanced Structural Adjustment Facility (ESAF) of loans worth $240 million (144 billion Tanzanian shillings) over three years.
Under the terms of the ESAF, Tanzania will receive $70 million in budgetary support soft loans for 1997, of which the first tranche totalling $40 million was paid in January.
Tanzania's President Benjamin Mkapa says he is committed to reforming the bloated civil service and the economy of a country which until 1985 followed a rigorous socialist economic policy.
The NBC, the largest commercial bank, has been kept afloat since 1992 by the injection of $3.3 million of government bonds from the central bank, according to a report given to the national assembly.
Despite the infusion of capital, the NBC continued to have financial difficulties, the report said.
The bank was divided into three components in January in a move the government said was necessary to ensure its future profitability.
The IMF team would also scrutinise the running of the People's Bank of Zanzibar (PBZ), the island's equivalent of the NBC, Osunsade said.
"People tend to forget it, but it was part of the ESAF agreement," he said. Earlier ESAF credit extended for budgetary support was severed in 1992 after a tax scandal.
The Paris Club of creditor nations agreed in January to give Tanzania reduction on debt repayments of up to 67 percent, the most generous terms available to the world's poorest nations.
Tanzania's annual inflation stands at 15.4 percent and its gross domestic product grew by about four percent in 1995.
One of the world's poorest countries, Tanzania has a reputation for stable democracy and vastly under-exploited potential in minerals, agriculture and tourism. ($1=600 Tanzanian shillings)
